\begin{proof}
Suppose first that $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ has a modulus of continuity $\mu$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta>0$ such that $0<s<\delta$ implies $\mu(s)<\varepsilon$. Then, whenever $x,y\in[a,b]$ and $|x-y|<\delta$, we have
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\leq \mu(|x-y|)<\varepsilon.
\]
Thus $f$ is uniformly continuous.

Conversely, suppose that $f$ is uniformly continuous. Define
\[
\omega(r)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:x,y\in[a,b],\ |x-y|\le r\},\qquad r>0.
\]
Uniform continuity implies that $\omega(r)\to0$ as $r\to0^+$. Also, $\omega$ is nondecreasing and finite, since $f$ is bounded on the compact interval $[a,b]$.

We use the elementary fact that every finite, nondecreasing function $\omega:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\omega(r)\to0$ as $r\to0^+$ has a continuous strictly increasing majorant $\mu:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ such that $\mu(r)\to0$ as $r\to0^+$. Indeed, choose a decreasing sequence $r_n\to0$ with $\omega(r_n)<2^{-n}$, join suitable points $(r_n,2^{-n})$ by line segments, and extend the resulting polygonal function strictly increasingly to $(0,\infty)$ above $\omega$.

For this $\mu$, if $x,y\in[a,b]$, then
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\omega(|x-y|)\leq\mu(|x-y|).
\]
Hence $\mu$ is a modulus of continuity for $f$. Therefore $f$ is uniformly continuous if and only if it has a modulus of continuity.
\end{proof}

\omega(r)\le\mu(r)\quad(r>0),

\[
